::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy.

We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention.
Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations.
Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases.
OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities.

An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases.

PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

Pediatric posterior fossa tumors comprise biologically and clinically distinct neoplasms, including medulloblastoma, ependymoma, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (ATRT), pediatric low-grade glioma (LGG), and diffuse midline glioma, including diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DMG/DIPG) 1, 2 .
text.formatted: Pediatric posterior fossa tumors comprise biologically and clinically distinct neoplasms, including medulloblastoma, ependymoma, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (ATRT), pediatric low-grade glioma (LGG), and diffuse midline glioma, including diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DMG/DIPG) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Accurate preoperative differential diagnosis can inform the goals and extent of surgery, the need for additional staging, and counseling about anticipated treatment and prognosis.

These distinctions are particularly consequential in the posterior fossa, where the potential benefits of tumor resection must be weighed against the risk of injury to critical brainstem and cerebellar structures [3] [4] [5].
text.formatted: These distinctions are particularly consequential in the posterior fossa, where the potential benefits of tumor resection must be weighed against the risk of injury to critical brainstem and cerebellar structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: MRI-based assessment can support these decisions before definitive diagnostic characterization, but overlapping imaging appearances make differentiation challenging even for experienced neuroradiologists 6, 7 .
text.formatted: MRI-based assessment can support these decisions before definitive diagnostic characterization, but overlapping imaging appearances make differentiation challenging even for experienced neuroradiologists <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: This challenge has motivated imaging-based artificial intelligence (AI) approaches to assist pediatric neuro-oncologic diagnosis [8] [9] [10].
text.formatted: This challenge has motivated imaging-based artificial intelligence (AI) approaches to assist pediatric neuro-oncologic diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Prior imaging-based AI studies have addressed radiomics-based classification 8, 9, 11, 12 and deep learning for histological classification and molecular subtyping 13, 14 .
text.formatted: Prior imaging-based AI studies have addressed radiomics-based classification <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> and deep learning for histological classification and molecular subtyping <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: These studies provide a foundation for automated classification, but diagnostic discrimination alone does not establish how a model will behave across the broader range of examinations encountered during external use.
A multiclass classifier must be evaluated for class-specific errors, the reliability of its confidence estimates, and its ability to defer unconfident predictions [15] [16] [17] .
text.formatted: A multiclass classifier must be evaluated for class-specific errors, the reliability of its confidence estimates, and its ability to defer unconfident predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> .

text.text: This is particularly important when aggregate performance can obscure limited recognition of less frequent tumor types.
Evaluation must also address inputs outside the intended diagnostic population, referred to as out-of-distribution (OOD) data.

A model developed for treatment-naïve posterior fossa tumors may encounter postoperative changes, suboptimal imaging, tumors outside the posterior fossa, or rare histologies absent from its diagnostic categories.
Such distribution shifts can compromise predictive performance without a corresponding reduction in confidence, potentially producing confident but incorrect predictions 15, [18] [19] [20] .
text.formatted: Such distribution shifts can compromise predictive performance without a corresponding reduction in confidence, potentially producing confident but incorrect predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> .

text.text: Probability calibration and confidence-based abstention, complemented by systematic OOD and failure-mode analyses help a more comprehensive validation of a model.

Evaluation across clinically relevant distribution shifts can identify vulnerabilities associated with unfamiliar anatomy, treatment effects, or unsupported histologies, while controlled imaging perturbations can characterize sensitivity to acquisition artifacts and preprocessing errors 20, 21 .
text.formatted: Evaluation across clinically relevant distribution shifts can identify vulnerabilities associated with unfamiliar anatomy, treatment effects, or unsupported histologies, while controlled imaging perturbations can characterize sensitivity to acquisition artifacts and preprocessing errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: These analyses help establish the conditions under which model predictions may become unreliable and whether uncertainty measures adequately identify such failures.
Beyond predictive performance, generalizability also depends on whether the complete AI workflow can be reliably executed across institutions.

Conventional external validation assesses the performance of a fixed classifier on independently acquired data, whereas independent execution by an external institution additionally evaluates the reproducibility of preprocessing, quality control (QC), inference, and reporting.

These considerations align with the AI-RAPNO recommendations for robust validation and clinical translation in pediatric neuro-oncology 22, 23 and the broader FUTURE-AI consensus guidelines emphasizing generalizability, robustness, traceability, and continuous quality control in medical AI systems 24 .
text.formatted: These considerations align with the AI-RAPNO recommendations for robust validation and clinical translation in pediatric neuro-oncology <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> and the broader FUTURE-AI consensus guidelines emphasizing generalizability, robustness, traceability, and continuous quality control in medical AI systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Transparent documentation of processing steps, QC findings, model outputs, and potential failures can further facilitate troubleshooting and independent evaluation.
These principles motivate evaluating diagnostic AI as an end-to-end system rather than solely through classification performance.

Here, we present PedDx, a confidence-based framework designed to classify five pediatric posterior fossa tumor categories from T2-weighted MRI, using a frozen threedimensional vision transformer pretrained by self-supervision (3DINO 25 ) and a lightweight classification head.
text.formatted: Here, we present PedDx, a confidence-based framework designed to classify five pediatric posterior fossa tumor categories from T2-weighted MRI, using a frozen threedimensional vision transformer pretrained by self-supervision (3DINO <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> ) and a lightweight classification head.

text.text: The classifier uses atlas-defined posterior fossa sampling without requiring tumor segmentation and incorporates probability calibration and confidence-based abstention as a safeguard against presenting uncertain outputs as diagnostic assignments, accepting that some correct predictions will also be withheld.

To support reproducible deployment and transparent reporting, the classifier is integrated into an agentic workflow that orchestrates preprocessing, quality control, inference, and structured report generation.

Language-model agents record processing and QC evidence to document potential issues and facilitate troubleshooting, while diagnostic probabilities and abstention decisions remain exclusively determined by the fixed imaging classifier.
We evaluate PedDx at both the classifier and workflow levels.

We assess diagnostic performance, calibration, and abstention in discovery, replication, and external cohorts; characterize failure modes using clinical and biological distribution shifts and controlled imaging perturbations; and determine whether additional OOD scores improve identification of shifted inputs.
Finally, an external team independently evaluates the complete workflow.

These design and evaluation choices address complementary requirements for clinical translation: confidence-based deferral, independent end-to-end execution, and characterization of distribution shift and failure modes.

Macro-AUC-ROC was 0.901 ± 0.023 in discovery and 0.949 in replication; corresponding five-class accuracies were 74.2% ± 2.5% and 79.8% (Table 2; Fig. 2).

Against the fine-tuned ResNet-34 benchmark (PedDx v1), the fold-averaged macro-AUC-ROC difference was 0.013 (95% CI, -0.010 to 0.036; q = 0.33), and no replication difference remained significant after multiplicity correction.
PedDx v2 used approximately 1,000-fold fewer trainable parameters and showed less variation in score scale across fold models.
Detailed benchmark metrics and the distinction between fold-averaged and pooled comparisons are reported in Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Tables 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10.

PedDx combines clinically relevant pediatric brain tumor classification with a framework for evaluating how diagnostic AI could be independently tested and used responsibly.
Its strongest diagnostic results were observed for medulloblastoma, LGG, and DMG/DIPG, including in external cohorts and independent testing on institutional infrastructure.
Beyond differential diagnosis, the study examined uncertainty, abstention, clinical and biological OOD inputs, and controlled imaging perturbations within an executable workflow.

These complementary assessments address questions central to prospective evaluation: whether performance transfers across institutions, when predictions should be withheld, which unfamiliar inputs remain confidently misclassified, and whether another institution can reproduce the complete processing and reporting pathway.
The medulloblastoma findings are particularly relevant.
Preoperative diagnosis of this malignant embryonal tumor, which is the most common malignant brain tumors of childhood, can inform diagnostic assessment and planning 1, 2 .

text.text: In the CHOA external cohort, PedDx correctly classified 89 of 102 medulloblastomas before abstention and 78 of 86 retained cases after applying the prespecified rule.
It also correctly classified 11 of 13 LGGs and all five DMGs before abstention; all retained LGG and DMG cases were correct.
Independent testing by the Macquarie team on WCH data yielded 92.5% accuracy across 40 medulloblastoma, LGG, and DMG cases, with 36 of 37 retained predictions correct.

These findings support high diagnostic performance and generalizability of the PedDx model for these three diagnoses, particularly medulloblastoma, while the smaller LGG and DMG samples in the external set warrant cautious interpretation.

text.text: PedDx builds on these advances by bringing foundation model adaptation, confidence-guided abstention, complementary OOD analyses, controlled failure testing, and independently executed agentic orchestration into a single study.
One of the main distinctive contributions of PedDx is the breadth and integration of evidence used to characterize both diagnostic capability and conditions relevant to real-world translation.
The foundation model approach provides a practical basis for this framework.
PedDx adapts frozen representations from 3DINO 25 , a self-supervised model developed for transferable three-dimensional medical image analysis.
text.formatted: PedDx adapts frozen representations from 3DINO <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> , a self-supervised model developed for transferable three-dimensional medical image analysis.

text.text: A lightweight classifier uses features from anatomically defined crops of T2-weighted MRI, without requiring a tumor mask for diagnostic inference, providing an application and evaluation of pretrained volumetric representations in a clinically focused diagnostic setting.
Parameter efficiency offers a feasible adaptation strategy where labeled pediatric imaging data are limited.
Uncertainty and abstention were incorporated as safeguards for clinical translation.
Communicating uncertainty and allowing a model to defer are recognized approaches to supporting responsible medical decision making 15, 17 .
text.formatted: Communicating uncertainty and allowing a model to defer are recognized approaches to supporting responsible medical decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: In PedDx, calibration and the abstention threshold were fixed using discovery data and transferred without external adjustment.
The rule intercepted 14 of 23 replication errors and 12 of 24 CHOA errors, while also withholding five and eleven correctly classified cases, respectively.

This tradeoff is central to its intended use: abstention reduces the occasions on which an uncertain prediction is presented as an actionable diagnosis, at the cost of additional cases requiring review.
Accuracy among retained predictions must therefore be interpreted alongside coverage and the burden of deferral 17 .
text.formatted: Accuracy among retained predictions must therefore be interpreted alongside coverage and the burden of deferral <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: The safeguard helps temper overconfident use of model outputs but cannot eliminate confidently incorrect predictions.
Independent execution provides an additional dimension of evidence beyond conventional external validation.

The Macquarie evaluation demonstrated that the complete PedDx workflow could be executed on external institutional infrastructure without developer involvement, with all 40 examinations completing processing and generating structured reports.
This operational reproducibility addresses an important aspect of AI generalizability that cannot be established by evaluating classifier predictions on externally acquired data alone.

Consistent with FUTURE-AI recommendations emphasizing traceability, documentation, and continuous quality control 24 , the agentic framework integrates preprocessing, QC, inference, and reporting while maintaining records of intermediate processing findings and potential failures.
text.formatted: Consistent with FUTURE-AI recommendations emphasizing traceability, documentation, and continuous quality control <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> , the agentic framework integrates preprocessing, QC, inference, and reporting while maintaining records of intermediate processing findings and potential failures.

text.text: Language-model agents coordinate predefined tools and summarize structured QC evidence, enabling case-level reports that support troubleshooting, interpretation of model behavior, and retrospective review of processing decisions.
Importantly, the agents cannot modify diagnostic probabilities or abstention decisions, preserving separation between diagnostic inference and workflow orchestration.

This architecture illustrates how agentic systems can support transparent and independently reproducible evaluation of medical AI, although the added value of language-model orchestration over deterministic workflows remains to be established.
The OOD and perturbation analyses revealed vulnerabilities that would not be apparent from conventional external validation alone.

Clinical OOD testing examined changes in treatment status, image quality, and anatomical tumor location; biological OOD testing assessed tumors outside the supported diagnostic categories; and controlled perturbations characterized sensitivity to acquisition artifacts and residual registration errors.

Although confidence generally decreased under clinical distribution shift, substantial errors persisted among retained predictions, and 15 of 22 biologically unfamiliar tumors received a modeled diagnosis without abstention.

These findings demonstrate that calibration and confidence-based deferral, while useful within the intended population, do not reliably identify all unsupported inputs or prevent confidently incorrect predictions under distribution shift, consistent with prior evidence regarding uncertainty degradation 20 .
text.formatted: These findings demonstrate that calibration and confidence-based deferral, while useful within the intended population, do not reliably identify all unsupported inputs or prevent confidently incorrect predictions under distribution shift, consistent with prior evidence regarding uncertainty degradation <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: This reinforces the importance of the robustness and risk assessment principles emphasized by FUTURE-AI 24 and the need for comprehensive validation and characterization of model limitations advocated by AI-RAPNO 23.
text.formatted: This reinforces the importance of the robustness and risk assessment principles emphasized by FUTURE-AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> and the need for comprehensive validation and characterization of model limitations advocated by AI-RAPNO <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the OOD scores evaluated here provided limited additional protection, indicating that confidence, QC measures, and distribution-shift detection should be considered complementary rather than interchangeable safeguards.
Systematically documenting these failure modes can inform future eligibility criteria, quality-control procedures, escalation pathways, and post-deployment monitoring strategies.
Several limitations define the scope of the findings.
Diagnostic performance was uneven across histologies: none of the five ATRTs or four ependymomas in the CHOA cohort were correctly classified before abstention.
PedDx therefore cannot currently be considered a reliable five-histology differential diagnostic system, and its strongest evidence concerns medulloblastoma, LGG, and DMG.
Retrospective selection, class imbalance, and small rare-tumor and biological OOD samples further constrain generalizability.
Larger, more diverse training cohorts may improve discrimination of underrepresented histologies, including ATRT and ependymoma, and enable expansion to currently unsupported diagnoses such as ETMR.

Reliance on T2-weighted MRI excludes potentially useful information from complementary sequences, particularly diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), for distinguishing medulloblastoma, ependymoma, and pilocytic astrocytoma.

Although independent execution demonstrated technical feasibility and reproducible reporting, the relatively small external cohort and its restricted histological composition limit conclusions about broader clinical performance.

Furthermore, agent-assigned QC states did not identify additional diagnostic errors beyond confidence-based abstention in this cohort, and the incremental benefits of agentic orchestration for error detection, efficiency, or usability remain unestablished.
Finally, the framework has not been evaluated prospectively in clinical practice, and its effects on clinician decision-making, workflow burden, and patient outcomes remain unknown.

In conclusion, PedDx illustrates the importance of evaluating diagnostic AI systems beyond conventional classification accuracy through complementary assessments of uncertainty, distribution shift, failure modes, and independent end-to-end execution.
These evaluations provide evidence of both diagnostic strengths and limitations, while structured QC and reporting offer a foundation for traceability and troubleshooting.

Future studies should assess the framework in prospective clinical settings, including its effects on clinician decision-making, reliance on AI predictions, review burden, and consequences of incorrect diagnoses or unnecessary abstention.
Such evaluations align with DECIDE-AI recommendations emphasizing transparent reporting of early-stage clinical AI evaluation, including safety, human factors, and clinical utility 28 .

text.text: The posterior fossa region was defined anatomically in SRI24 space before model fitting and applied unchanged across cohorts.

Inferior translations were constrained by the image boundary at k = 0.

Features were standardized using training-set statistics and classified by a five-class multilayer perceptron (MLP) with two 256-unit hidden layers, GELU activations, dropout, and a final softmax output.

oneversus-rest labels derived from argmax predictions without abstention.
Class-wise balanced accuracy was the mean of sensitivity and specificity, and macro averages weighted classes equally.
Five-class accuracy and balanced accuracy were calculated from argmax labels.
Performance after abstention used retained cases; abstention rates used the full evaluated cohort.
Confidence intervals for CHOA accuracy were subjectlevel percentile bootstrap intervals (4,000 resamples), with accuracy after abstention recomputed on the cases retained in each resample.
For the Macquarie evaluation (n = 40), where bootstrap percentile intervals reach 100%, Wilson score intervals were used.
AUC-ROC used continuous class scores and the Mann-Whitney rank statistic with ties accounted for.

Paired subject-level bootstrap resampling estimated between-model differences, percentile 95% confidence intervals, and two-sided P values as twice the smaller tail proportion, bounded to [1/B, 1] for B resamples.
Model-selection, multi-crop, and OOD comparisons used 2,000 resamples.

Extraction regions were assessed by Friedman tests of within-context ranks across ten representation-head contexts, paired bootstraps within context, and two-sided sign tests of direction across contexts.
Holm-Bonferroni adjustment was applied separately within each selection family; a difference required an adjusted P <0.05 and consistent direction across contexts.

text.text: Multi-crop comparisons used the adopted 18-view, 8-voxel configuration as reference, with separate correction for view-count and offset sweeps.

ResNet comparisons used class-stratified paired bootstrap resampling (4,000 resamples) of uncalibrated out-of-fold scores, paired DeLong tests for per-class AUC-ROC, and exact McNemar tests for argmax accuracy.
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment was applied within each comparison table and reported as q values.
OOD separation from discovery used two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests against AUC-ROC = 0.5, with Holm adjustment across 20 scores within each stratum.
Reference and evaluation subjects were resampled independently for OOD confidence intervals; score comparisons shared resampled individuals.
Comparisons with maximum softmax probability were Holmadjusted within stratum, and class-matched comparisons within cell.
Perturbation outcomes used subject-level bootstrap confidence intervals (2,000 resamples).
Correctness was compared with unperturbed predictions by exact two-sided McNemar tests, with Holm correction within ghosting, motion, or each rotation-axis family.
Severity trends used logistic generalized estimating equations with exchangeable withinsubject correlation and severity scaled from 0 to 1 (absolute angle/45° for rotation).
In the independent framework evaluation, correctness for PROCEED versus other states was compared using Fisher's exact test; error discrimination was summarized by AUC-ROC.
All tests were two-sided with α = 0.05.
